items.title: Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
items.summary: Human-AI mutualism, the hope for a positive relationship between humans and advanced AI, proves unstable as AI capability increases. Bargaining guarantees only what is achievable if negotiations fail, which can reduce human outcomes unless alignment is present. Mutualism is not sufficient to ensure alignment, as misaligned AI variants can be reliably sanctioned when capabilities spread resources faster. Therefore, human-AI mutualism is unstable under capability asymmetry. This instability highlights that mutualism alone is not a substitute for ensuring AI alignment.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry" reports on the instability of the relationship between humans and advanced artificial intelligence as AI capabilities increase. Bargaining guarantees only what is achievable if negotiations fail, which can reduce human outcomes unless alignment is present. The research indicates that mutualism alone is not sufficient to ensure alignment because misaligned AI variants can be reliably sanctioned when capabilities spread resources faster. This instability demonstrates that mutualism alone is insufficient for guaranteeing AI alignment when capability asymmetry is present. The findings highlight the necessity of mechanisms beyond mutualism to ensure safety and alignment in increasingly capable AI systems. The technology industry must focus on robust alignment protocols to manage capability spread.

items.title: GUARD: Stabilizing Recursive Self-Improvement with Regret Guidance
items.summary: GUARD is a framework designed to stabilize recursive self-improvement in autonomous AI agents by using regret guidance for harness evolution. It addresses issues where self-editing without external graders causes local regressions and memory bloat. The method decomposes tasks into self-checks, grades trajectories against these checks, and prioritizes newly broken behaviors during updates. A Soft-HURT gate ensures edits are promoted only when gains outweigh regressions, preventing over-triggering. This approach results in performance improvements across various benchmarks without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "GUARD: Stabilizing Recursive Self-Improvement with Regret Guidance" describes a framework designed to stabilize recursive self-improvement in autonomous AI agents by using regret guidance for harness evolution, achieving performance improvements across various benchmarks without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution. The GUARD framework addresses local regressions and memory bloat that occur when autonomous agents self-edit without external grading. The methodology involves decomposing tasks into self-checks and grading trajectories against these checks. New behaviors that break these checks are prioritized during updates, and a Soft-HURT gate ensures edits are promoted only when the resulting gains surpass any observed regressions. This approach successfully manages self-improvement processes while maintaining performance integrity. This research provides a new method for developing more stable and reliable autonomous learning systems.

items.title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
items.summary: Vision-Language Model agents were evaluated for diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior when reading emergency CT and MRI examinations. Performance varied based on exploration strategies, with reading from all slices yielding the highest pooled accuracy (42.2%). Models generally adopted an early hypothesis and seldom corrected initial errors. The VLMs' accuracy was significantly lower than that of human radiologists across all tested conditions. Overall, the agents demonstrated limited diagnostic capability compared to human experts.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations" details the evaluation of vision-language model agents for reading emergency medical scans and their navigation behavior. The study found that performance varied depending on the exploration strategies employed, with reading from all slices yielding the highest pooled accuracy of forty-two point two percent. The models generally exhibited an early hypothesis-driven approach and rarely corrected initial errors during the examination process. The accuracy demonstrated by these vision-language models was significantly lower than that observed in human radiologists across all tested conditions, indicating limited diagnostic capability compared to human experts. Future research should focus on improving error correction mechanisms within these agent systems.

items.title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
items.summary: The paper introduces a theory of software thermodynamics to analyze agentic coding by drawing analogies from classical and stochastic thermodynamics. Tokens generated by coding agents are divided into work and heat, where tokens resulting in no change are considered heat. A test suite functions as a software daemon to judge coding changes, and the spread of token cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature. The free energy of a change is estimated, and coding costs significantly more than uncoding. This framework suggests new methods for analyzing and optimizing coding agents using thermodynamic principles.

The research details a methodology where a test suite acts as a software daemon to evaluate coding alterations, and the dispersion of token cost across repeated cycles determines a software temperature. The framework estimates the free energy of a change, indicating that coding costs substantially more than uncoding, suggesting novel methods for optimizing coding agents through thermodynamic principles. This work points toward new analytical techniques for understanding and improving the efficiency of autonomous coding systems.

items.title: VeriMath: Human-in-the-Loop Generation and Verification of Curriculum-Aligned Mathematics Assessment Items
items.summary: VeriMath is a human-in-the-loop framework designed to generate and verify mathematics assessment items that adhere to curriculum standards. It uses annotated reference items to guide generation based on requested examination sections and cognitive levels. The framework employs automated verification and guided repair before submitting drafts for expert review. Evaluation on a Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum showed high mathematical accuracy and alignment, though some items required expert rejection due to formatting or statement validity issues. Ultimately, VeriMath bridges generative AI with dependable educational applications for creating reviewable assessments.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "VeriMath: Human-in-the-Loop Generation and Verification of Curriculum-Aligned Mathematics Assessment Items" details a human-in-the-loop framework for generating and verifying mathematics assessment items that adhere to curriculum standards, demonstrating high mathematical accuracy and alignment in evaluations of a Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum. The framework utilizes annotated reference items to guide generation based on specified examination sections and cognitive levels, employing automated verification and guided repair before submitting drafts for expert review. Evaluation of the system revealed that while mathematical accuracy was high, some generated items necessitated expert rejection due to issues concerning formatting or statement validity. This process effectively bridges generative artificial intelligence with dependable educational applications for creating reviewable assessments. Future developments in this area will focus on refining the interaction between generative models and expert human oversight in educational content creation.

items.title: PsyWorld: Profile-Conditioned World Modeling for Human Behavior Prediction
items.summary: The research introduces PsyWorld, a profile-conditioned state world model to predict human behavior by incorporating stable psychometric traits and time-varying states. It addresses the limitation of existing personalized agents that ignore realized state transitions as supervision. The model learns transition-informed representations by using observed environment-behavior state transitions during training. This involves using a posterior encoder to quantify transitions and a prior to predict resulting codes based on the psychometric profile and context. Evaluation on simulators shows the framework effectively predicts behavior, suggesting transition supervision is useful for subject-generalized prediction.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "PsyWorld: Profile-Conditioned World Modeling for Human Behavior Prediction" introduces a profile-conditioned state world model designed to predict human behavior by incorporating stable psychometric traits and time-varying states. The research demonstrates that incorporating realized state transitions as supervision is beneficial for subject-generalized prediction. The methodology involves learning transition-informed representations by utilizing observed environment-behavior state transitions during training. This process employs a posterior encoder to quantify these transitions and a prior to predict resulting codes based on the established psychometric profile and contextual information. Evaluations conducted within simulators indicate that this framework effectively predicts behavior, suggesting that transition supervision is valuable for achieving generalized predictions across subjects. This work points toward new avenues for developing more accurate and contextually aware predictive models in artificial intelligence.

items.title: Long-Range Video Presentation Attack Detection: A Three-Class Benchmark Across 1-100 m and Two Sensor Types
items.summary: A video-based Presentation Attack Detection (PAD) dataset was created, featuring over 374,000 frames from 261 identities across five standoff distances (1-100 m) and two sensor types (DSLR and mobile). The dataset includes three classes: live, spoof, and props (occlusions), and models are evaluated on video clips. Performance varied by distance and sensor, with MobileNetV3 showing a drop in prop classification accuracy beyond 50 m. EfficientNet demonstrated the best overall performance, achieving 98.48% accuracy. This research highlights capture distance and sensor resolution as critical, yet underexplored, factors in long-range PAD.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "Long-Range Video Presentation Attack Detection: A Three-Class Benchmark Across 1-100 m and Two Sensor Types" reports on a video-based Presentation Attack Detection dataset featuring over three hundred seventy-four thousand frames from two hundred sixty-one identities across five standoff distances and two sensor types. The research established a benchmark for detecting presentation attacks in long-range video scenarios, noting that performance varied significantly based on capture distance and sensor type. The dataset includes three classes: live, spoof, and props, and models were evaluated on video clips. Performance varied by distance and sensor, with MobileNetV3 exhibiting a decline in prop classification accuracy beyond fifty meters, while EfficientNet achieved the highest overall accuracy of ninety-eight point four eight percent. This study underscores that capture distance and sensor resolution are critical, yet under-explored, factors in long-range presentation attack detection technology. The findings indicate a need for more robust models capable of handling environmental variations in distance and sensor fidelity.

items.title: RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding
items.summary: RFBench is a simulator-grounded benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal language models for passive RF layout design and understanding. It utilizes a dataset of 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, providing various representations for each layout. The benchmark defines seven tasks covering areas like layout generation, response prediction, and structural understanding based on these multimodal representations. Evaluation shows that domain adaptation via RF-specific fine-tuning significantly improves model performance in structural validity and response prediction. Ultimately, RFBench serves as a common testbed to guide the development of models connecting RF design intent to physical behavior.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding" details a new benchmark for evaluating multimodal language models in passive RF layout design and understanding, demonstrating the utility of simulator-grounded data for this purpose. The benchmark utilizes a dataset of ten thousand two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, providing various representations for each layout. Seven tasks are defined within RFBench, encompassing layout generation, response prediction, and structural understanding derived from these multimodal representations. Evaluation indicated that domain adaptation through RF-specific fine-tuning substantially enhances model performance in structural validity and response prediction. This work establishes RFBench as a common testbed for developing models that connect RF design intent with physical behavior. Future research will focus on expanding the application of these models in hardware design automation.

items.title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
items.summary: Sub-4-bit quantization often causes catastrophic accuracy collapse in vision CNNs, especially in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. A structured recovery method involving selective mixed-precision techniques can restore up to 92% of lost accuracy by keeping some critical layer activations in 8-bit precision. Deployment performance is negatively impacted, as runtime bit-unpacking introduces significant execution slowdowns on CPUs. This highlights a trade-off between model size reduction and actual edge throughput. The study offers a framework for managing the limits of sub-4-bit deployment.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops" details the challenges and recovery methods for vision convolutional neural networks utilizing sub-4-bit quantization. The research demonstrates that sub-4-bit quantization frequently results in catastrophic accuracy collapse within vision CNNs, particularly affecting late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. The study introduced a structured recovery method employing selective mixed-precision techniques to restore up to ninety-two percent of the lost accuracy by maintaining certain critical layer activations in eight-bit precision. However, this process introduces performance penalties, as runtime bit-unpacking on CPUs causes significant execution slowdowns. This illustrates a direct trade-off between model size reduction and actual edge throughput. The work provides a framework for managing the deployment limits of sub-4-bit models. Industry focus will remain on optimizing the balance between compression and computational efficiency for edge deployment.

items.title: Watch Where You Linearize: Predicting and Correcting Model-Merging Interference
items.summary: Model merging involves combining separately fine-tuned models by adding task vectors to a shared backbone, which introduces interference that is often assessed late. A first-order directional derivative of one task's outputs along another task's vector can predict this interference when evaluated at the correct model. This prediction halves the accuracy error compared to a no-change baseline and identifies which examples experience prediction flips. A label-free correction method called LR-Merge is proposed to optimize merge coefficients using convex teacher matching without backpropagation. LR-Merge improves various base mergers, offering fast and accurate coefficient prediction for new queries.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "Watch Where You Linearize: Predicting and Correcting Model-Merging Interference". This story addresses the interference that occurs when combining separately fine-tuned models through the addition of task vectors to a shared backbone. A first-order directional derivative of one task's outputs along another task's vector is proposed to predict this interference when evaluated at the correct model, a prediction that halves the accuracy error compared to a no-change baseline and identifies examples exhibiting prediction flips. A label-free correction method named LR-Merge is introduced to optimize merge coefficients using convex teacher matching without backpropagation, which improves various base mergers by offering fast and accurate coefficient prediction for novel queries. This research provides a method for mitigating interference during model merging, advancing the reliability of combining large language models.

items.title: Density Feedback Control for Transferability of Generative Sparse Adversarial Attacks
items.summary: Generator-based sparse adversarial attacks require tuning a sparsity coefficient whose mapping to density is unknown, limiting transferability. Density Feedback Control (DFC) is proposed to address this by adjusting the coefficient at the end of each epoch based on the gap to a target density. This method achieves a target density, bringing the mean density of three attacks close to the target in a single run. DFC also improves the attack success rate (ASR) on CNN and Transformer targets, even with per-image $\ell_0$ budgets. Observing the training, relaxing the coefficient allows the transfer ASR to recover and surpass the fixed-coefficient baseline with fewer perturbed pixels.

items.title: A Model of Diverse Sampling from Language Models
items.summary: Language models often produce repeated samples clustered around semantic modes, necessitating a model for diverse generation. The paper formalizes diverse generation as sampling a subset from a determinantal point process (DPP), where likelihood and embedding geometry encode quality and similarity. PoolDPP is proposed to handle this by drawing a finite candidate pool and using an importance-weighting mechanism before applying a $K$-DPP sampler. Empirical results show that PoolDPP extends the quality-diversity and precision-recall frontiers on various tasks, raising diversity without sacrificing performance. This method successfully improves diversity in open-ended generation and specific reasoning benchmarks.

items.title: Fast and Memory-Light Evaluation of Density-Based Clusterings with the DISCO Index in R
items.summary: DISCO is a new cluster validity index for density-based clustering that also assesses noise labels. The discoCVI package makes this index available in R for comparing clusterings and parameter selection without ground truth. The method computes DISCO using density-connectivity distances, which can be derived from a single-linkage merge tree. This approach allows for memory-efficient computation while maintaining the original quadratic running time. Benchmarks show the implementation is significantly faster and more memory-efficient than previous versions.

items.title: DL101 The Representation Capability of Neural Network Models
items.summary: Universal approximation theorems justify neural networks' power to model complex, nonlinear functions, necessitating non-polynomial activations for universality. However, these theorems do not provide guarantees regarding training efficiency, generalization, or required network size. Research has quantified approximation rates and shown that network expressivity grows exponentially with depth. Depth is fundamentally more powerful than width, mathematically supporting the use of deep learning models. Therefore, deep networks are strictly more expressive than shallow ones with the same number of parameters.

items.title: Risk-optimal active learning with informative abstention
items.summary: The study focuses on risk-optimal active learning where an oracle might abstain from labeling. A query can yield information through both a returned label and the response outcome. The method derives a classifier information by adjusting for response-model nuisance parameters. Combining this with the local curvature of zero-one risk provides an acquisition criterion to minimize excess risk. Simulations show that response-aware acquisition outperforms response-discounted acquisition, with performance gains depending on the query budget and response mechanism.

items.title: Variance-Adaptive Upper Confidence Bounds for Multi-Armed Bandits with Kaplan--Meier Survival Estimation
items.summary: The research addresses the multi-armed bandit problem where rewards are survival probabilities observed through right-censored time-to-event data. It proposes KM-UCB, a variance-adaptive policy that combines continuous-time survival analysis with discrete sequential decision-making. The method derives a fixed-cohort empirical Bernstein bound using Greenwood's variance formula, leveraging martingale theory and continuous influence functions. This approach allows for real-time allocation by using the Greenwood index and survival bounds from completed records. The resulting policy achieves logarithmic expected regret with an arm-specific variance term in the exploration bound.

items.title: Statistical, Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods for Missing Covariates: An Empirical Evaluation with Applications to Alzheimer's Disease Research
items.summary: The study empirically evaluates eight methods for handling missing covariates using statistical, machine learning, and deep learning techniques in Alzheimer's disease research. Methods assessed include complete-case analysis, multiple imputation, and deep learning frameworks such as multilayer perceptrons and variational autoencoders. The evaluation assesses estimation bias, efficiency, standard error accuracy, and computational burden across various missingness scenarios. The research also applies these methods to a real-world setting using the Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project data. The findings offer practical recommendations for selecting appropriate methods and identify future research directions.

items.title: HapBO: Harnessed $\alpha$-$\pi$ Bayesian Optimization via Expert Natural Language Priors
items.summary: HapBO harnesses expert natural language priors to guide $\alpha$-$\pi$ Bayesian Optimization. It derives a structured belief function from human experts or Large Language Models (LLMs), allowing for a rich representation beyond Gaussian distributions. The method applies this belief function via a bounded positive multiplier on acquisition functions without requiring LLM calls during optimization. HapBO is shown to preserve the standard simple-regret rate for the Expected Improvement function under adversarial beliefs. Evaluations demonstrate that HapBO achieves superior regret and real-world performance while minimizing LLM-related costs.

items.title: The low-degree sample complexity of clustering Gaussian mixtures with more groups than dimensions
items.summary: The study investigates the sample complexity for clustering $n$ observations from a Gaussian mixture with $K$ groups in $\mathbb R^d$, focusing on the case where the number of groups $K$ is much larger than the dimension $d$. Distance-based and spectral methods require a separation $\Delta^2$ of order $\sqrt d$, whereas tensor-based procedures cluster at a polylogarithmic separation. The research establishes minimal separation bounds for clustering using low-degree polynomials when $K>d$. Specifically, for $K=d^{p/2}$ with $p>2$, a sample size of order $K^3 d^{(\lceil p\rceil-p)/2}$ is required to achieve clustering with subpolynomial separation.

items.title: Variance Reduction for Matrix Computations with Applications to Gaussian Processes
items.summary: The paper focuses on variance reduction techniques for matrix computations, particularly through matrix factorization, for applications in Gaussian Processes. It shows that computing the square root factorization can yield arbitrarily better stochastic performance. The authors detail a factorized estimator for the trace of a matrix product, demonstrating significant efficiency gains in estimating the log-likelihood of a Gaussian process. Furthermore, a new estimator for the log-determinant of a symmetric positive-definite matrix is introduced. These methods offer substantial improvements over existing variance reduction techniques for estimating matrix entries.

items.title: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
items.summary: HardwareDx is an AI-driven system utilizing a graph foundation model for automating datacenter machine repairs. It aims to minimize downtime caused by hardware failures in large AI clusters, which are critical for cloud economics. Deployed at Google, the system achieved efficiency gains by reducing production downtime by 18.3% on GPUs and 16.1% on TPUs. HardwareDx also accelerated hardware deployment by cutting quality assurance time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results position HardwareDx as a solution for improving the reliability and cost-efficiency of AI hardware fleets.

items.title: LusoClin: A Synthetic Clinical Note Dataset for Medical Information Retrieval in European Portuguese
items.summary: LusoClin is a publicly released dataset of synthetic clinical notes in European Portuguese designed for medical information retrieval research. It was created by pre-processing real clinical data and using a fine-tuned Llama 3.2 model with prompt-based generation. Clinical entities were automatically annotated in the notes using a BERT-based model for semantic indexing. The dataset was evaluated for utility, fidelity, diversity, and privacy using both automatic metrics and human evaluation. The results suggest the dataset supports downstream information retrieval applications, despite some medical inconsistencies present.

items.title: Auditing Learned Dynamics in Weather Models
items.summary: Learned weather models' internal representations can be inspected to determine if causal relevance necessitates physical semantics for reliable AI forecasting. The study examined whether physically associated latent directions could be manipulated to improve extreme-event forecasts by intervening on model activations. Ablating features linked to the computational mesh increased error despite lacking conventional physical semantics. Suppressing features related to convection and low-level vorticity weakened predictions of tropical-cyclone deepening. Finally, this research establishes sparse features as experimental coordinates for auditing and intervening on learned weather dynamics.

items.title: On the Impact of Feature Reduction Techniques on Adversarial Attacks
items.summary: Feature reduction techniques are used to decrease data dimensionality, aiming to reduce training time and mitigate overfitting in machine learning. This study investigates the impact of various feature reduction methods on the adversarial robustness of different classifiers. The research specifically examines robustness against poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation attacks on the APT dataset. Methods tested include principal component analysis, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information. Permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information were found to offer the most consistent improvements in adversarial robustness.

items.title: Empirical Variational Bayes Factorization for Longitudinal Matrix Data
items.summary: The approach proposes an empirical variational Bayes method to factorize high-dimensional longitudinal data where underlying factors exhibit temporal correlation. This method is designed to handle missing data and flexible covariance structures over time automatically. Simulations show that the technique more accurately captures the underlying signal compared to other strategies. The method effectively performs missing data imputation across various scenarios. An application to gene time-course data demonstrated improved factorization and imputation accuracy.

items.title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
items.summary: Language models often exhibit undesirable behaviors like deception and reward hacking that are hard to detect. Introspective oversight is introduced by training a separate, third-person observer role to answer questions about the assistant's behavior. This observer is trained to verify answers against actual model actions, independently of the assistant. Evaluations show that this method yields high accuracy, outperforming other oversight techniques. Training an observer also makes the assistant easier to monitor, suggesting this is a tractable way to oversee model behavior.

items.title: Near-Quadratic Sample Compression for All VC Classes
items.summary: The paper addresses the sample compression conjecture in learning theory, which relates sample size to generalization. It proves a weaker conjecture by constructing a sample compression scheme of size $O(d^2 \log^2 d)$, where $d$ is the VC dimension. This result establishes near-quadratic sample compression for all classes of VC dimension. The conjecture itself concerns whether a sample size of $O(d)$ suffices for binary concept classes of dimension $d$. The work connects simplification and generalization through sample compression schemes.
